issues: The source promises a return and rule over oppressors; a visual of returning people is a reasonable inference, but should remain symbolic and not imply a specific historical event or identity.
The promised rest is future; the proposed image of people at rest is a symbolic visual inference, not a narrated present event.
The broken royal emblems are symbolic visual interpretation; avoid depicting a specific king, event, or proverb performance.
The earth’s rest and singing are poetic language; keep any broad visual symbolic and do not invent visible singers or a present persecution scene.
The trees’ rejoicing and speech are personification; the landscape is a reasonable inference, but should not imply literal talking trees.
The underworld gathering is prophetic imagery; avoid asserting literal afterlife geography or mechanics, and do not assign identities or appearances to the kings or fallen king.
The grave imagery is poetic; a grave, instrument, and worms are supported, but a specific visible corpse or literal staging is not established.
Observers looking at an unnamed fallen figure are a reasonable visual inference from those who see him; the pit’s appearance and all figures’ identities remain unspecified.
The contrast in burial status is supported, but the proposed symbolic visual should not concretely depict unidentified slain people or a specific manner of exclusion.
An abandoned, waterlogged Babylon is a symbolic inference from the prophecy, not an event narrated as occurring now; the threatened slaughter must not be depicted.
A lifted burden is a reasonable symbolic inference, but the prophecy does not establish a present scene, visible divine figure, or specific battle.
A distant smoke is supported as prophetic imagery, but its source and the creatures’ appearance are unspecified; do not make the serpent imagery a literal event.
A symbolic view of Zion is an inference only; the text does not specify its appearance or establish a present exchange among visible messengers.
